items.title: Marian McPartland interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, April 26, 1997
items.q: I’d heard of Bud Freeman and Sidney Bechet, but I hadn’t heard of Jimmy yet.

ctx.x: I wonder if there’s any pictures of that?

Unfortunately no. If I’d known what I was going to get into — I didn’t take pictures. Oh there are some, yeah there are some, but yeah there are some now that I think of it. But I should have kept a diary. And anyway we went through all of these miserably bombed and strafed towns that were just a mass of rubble, and we finally arrived in Belgium in a rest area, and it was called Eupen, and they had a big band and they had all kinds of stuff going on and the area shows would come there to rest, and they had an…
How do you play with a big band? I mean, to our piano players who will be watching.

items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I’d heard that Bud Freeman went to him and took some lessons. Bud Freeman was saying how interesting . . . in fact it was written up in Down Beat, like it was a happening. Bud Freeman studies with Lennie Tristano.

ctx.x: Yes. Was someone, and these can be little quick short answers, influenced, say someone like Lennie Tristano?

Yes. As a matter of fact I went and took . . . I took a lesson or two with Lennie Tristano. This was when Jimmy and I first came to New York. I thought he could help me improve my overall jazz playing. I’d heard that Bud Freeman went to him and took some lessons. Bud Freeman was saying how interesting . . . in fact it was written up in Down Beat, like it was a happening. Bud Freeman studies with Lennie Tristano. How bizarre can you be? Anyway, I thought I would go, and I went to see Lennie. I think I had met him…

said, if you want to be a romantic kind of player who plays rubato and goes with the . . . you just flow back and forth, you don’t keep a steady rhythm, that’s fine. But if you want to be a jazz player and have good time, you better go home and play with the metronome. That was pretty much what he said. I was crushed, but I felt that it was a valid criticism, and I did that.

items.title: 66100_Bud Freeman oral history interview
items.q: I was to meet the McPartland brothers, Jimmy who is still going very strong, of course, married to Marian Mary McPartland

ctx.x: Well, of course, it was not until I was about 15 that I was to meet at Austin High School, I was to meet the McPartland brothers, Jimmy who is still going very strong, of course, married to Marian Mary McPartland, who is by the way coming over here to England and had a marvelous musical career. I saw Jimmy at Nice last year and he was just as good as ever and in wonderful condition.

Well, anyway, it was through Jimmy's effort that (You know,) I got a saxophone because he went to my dad and he said, I think Bud, he sings and he dances and I think he might have a natural talent for playing and why don't you consider buying him a C-Melody saxophone. That was the instrument one started on, I was not to continue that. We didn't know whether I could really get into playing, so now in the meantime before any of this happened Dave Tough, the great drummer, later to become I thought the best, with…
